## Abstract

This paper describes the open-source code Enzo, which uses block-structured adaptive mesh refinement to provide high spatial and temporal resolution for modeling astrophysical fluid flows. The code is Cartesian, can be run in 1, 2, and 3 dimensions, and supports a wide variety of physics including hydrodynamics, ideal and non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics, N-body dynamics (and, more broadly, self-gravity of fluids and particles), primordial gas chemistry, optically-thin radiative cooling of primordial and metal-enriched plasmas (as well as some optically-thick cooling models), radiation transport, cosmological expansion, and models for star formation and feedback in a cosmological context. In addition to explaining the algorithms implemented, we present solutions for a wide range of test problems, demonstrate the code's parallel performance, and discuss the Enzo collaboration's code development methodology.

L46@P1: (SMBH) are now strongly believed to lurk at the centers of probably every massive galaxy
L47@P1: (Magorrian et al. 1998; Ferrarese & Merritt 2000; Gebhardt et al. 2000; Tremaine et al.
L48@P1: 2002). One of the most prominent known forms of feedback from the growth of SMBH that
L49@P1: is mechanically tightly coupled to surrounding gas is the powerful radio jets and giant radio
L50@P1: lobes, whose energy is often observed to exceed 105−6 M⊙c
L51@P1: 2
L52@P1: ergs (Urry 2000; Kronberg et al.
L53@P1: 2001). Therefore, there is a good reason to believe that the inclusion of Active Galactic Nuclei
L54@P1: (AGN) feedback, in form of radio jets/lobes, in direct simulations may bring theoretical
L55@P1: predictions into good agreement with observations. In this case, our understanding of X-ray
L56@P1: cluster formation will be much more complete and physically sound, which in turn would
L57@P1: allow us to remove systematic uncertainties with regard to determinations of dark matter and
L58@P1: dark energy, among others, afforded by accumulating X-ray data and upcoming SunyaevZel’dovich (SZ) cluster data. Clearly, it has become very pressing to properly model AGN
L59@P1: feedback in cosmological simulations.
L60@P1: In this era of precision cosmology, multiple, independent constraints on cosmological
L61@P1: parameters are vital. Weak gravitational lensing of galaxies by large-scale structure provides
L62@P1: one of the most powerful probes of matter distribution in the Universe (e.g., Refregier 2003).
L63@P1: Since weak lensing directly probes the mass distribution, which is dominated by dark matter,
L64@P1: it is often assumed that baryonic physics is not that important. With powerful future weak
L65@P1-2: lensing surveys such as PanSTARRS, SNAP and LSST, which have the potential capability– 3 –
L66@P2: of reducing statistical errors to about 1% level with regard to power spectrum and dark
L67@P2: energy equation-of-state determinations, it will be necessary to understand hitherto “less
L68@P2: important” effects such as the physics of cosmic baryons. Baryons constitute a significant
L69@P2: fraction (∼ 17%) of total mass in the Universe (Spergel et al. 2006) and could make a
L70@P2: significant contribution to the total matter power spectrum. On sub-megaparsec scales,
L71@P2: baryons are known to be subject to different physics than the dark matter, and important
L72@P2: differences between distributions of baryons and dark matter on small scales (≤ 100kpc)
L73@P2: are well observed, such as in our own galaxy. It is, however, often assumed that baryons
L74@P2: follow dark matter on large scales (≥ 1Mpc), where signals of weak gravitational lensing by
L75@P2: large-scale structure are detected to in turn determine the total matter distribution on these
L76@P2: large scales. Estimates based on observed radio-lobe energy from AGN suggest that a large
L77@P2: volume fraction of the intergalactic medium may be moved and filled with magnetic bubbles
L78@P2: (Furlanetto & Loeb 2001; Kronberg et al. 2001; Levine & Gnedin 2005). As a result, the
L79@P2: effect of large-scale movement of baryonic gas under the influence of giant radio lobes/jets
L80@P2: from AGN on the total matter power spectrum might be as large as 30% based on a simplified
L81@P2: spherical model (Levine & Gnedin 2006). While the exact effect on the intergalactic medium
L82@P2: of giant radio jet/lobes from AGN is presently highly uncertain due to lack of any adequate
L83@P2: treatment, these initial rough estimates of potential effects point to the need of much more
L84@P2: detailed investigations. It is prudent to re-examine with greater care the assumption that
L85@P2: baryons follow dark matter on large scales in light of the potential capabilities of future
L86@P2: weak lensing surveys. Cosmological parameters determined with claimed achievable high
L87@P2: statistical accuracy based on gravitational weak lensing can be realized only after systematic
L88@P2: effects on baryons due to powerful AGN feedback can be convincingly demonstrated and
L89@P2: removed. Magnetohydrodynamics simulations provide the necessary tools to tackle this
L90@P2: important problem.
L91@P2: The idea of AGN feedback is not new (e.g., Silk & Rees 1998; Kronberg et al. 2001;
L92@P2: Churazov et al. 2001; Quilis, Bower, & Balogh 2001; Bruggen & Kaiser 2001; Binney 2004;
L93@P2: Omma & Binney 2004; Ruszkowski, Bruggen & Begelman 2004; Henrik et al. 2004; Scannapieco & Oh 2004; Begelman 2004; Dalla Vecchia et al. 2004; Begelman & Ruszkowski
L94@P2: 2005; Bruggen, Ruszkowski, & Hallman 2005; Croton et al. 2006). Recent SPH (smoothedparticle-hydrodynamics) simulations have taken a major step to implement such an AGN
L95@P2: feedback (Hopkins et al. 2005a,b,c,d,2006; Robertson et al. 2006; Sajacki & Springel 2006)
L96@P2: through a deposition of thermal energy in the central regions of galaxies where massive gas
L97@P2: accretion onto the central SMBH takes place. The effects are clearly demonstrated to be
L98@P2: significant, often with dramatic effects, such as a complete sweep-out of interstellar medium.
L99@P2: But real MHD modeling is largely lacking. Undoubtedly radio jets are highly anisotropic
L100@P2-3: and the overall dynamics and thermodynamics of magnetic jets/bubbles and baryons on– 4 –
L101@P3: scales ranging from cluster cores to large-scale structure requires solving the propagation of
L102@P3: relativistic jets using cosmological MHD codes in a complex, dynamic, cosmological setting.
L103@P3: As an example, a highly collimated relativistic radio jet may not deposit most of its energy
L104@P3: in the immediate neighborhood, whereas a thermal and spherical deposition of the energy,
L105@P3: as has been implemented in SPH simulation, would cause an interaction with the immediate
L106@P3: surrounding gas at the outset.
L107@P3: It has been well established that there are widespread magnetic fields in the intracluster
L108@P3: medium (see Carilli & Taylor 2002; Govoni 2006 for recent reviews). There has also been
L109@P3: tantalizing evidence for magnetic fields in the wider intergalactic medium (IGM) (Kim et
L110@P3: al. 1989). The origin of these large-scale magnetic fields is still unknown though several
L111@P3: suggestions have been made (e.g., Kulsrud et al. 1997; Furlanetto & Loeb 2001; Kronberg et
L112@P3: al. 2001). Furthermore, it is presently mostly unknown whether these magnetic fields have
L113@P3: played an important role or not, in systems ranging from large-scale structure formation,
L114@P3: to galaxy clusters, to cluster core regions and to galaxy formation itself. There have been
L115@P3: some studies aimed at investigating the role of magnetic fields in the intracluster (ICM)
L116@P3: and IGM (Ryu et al. 1998; Dolag et al. 2002; Dolag et al. 2005; Br¨uggen et al. 2005).
L117@P3: Numerically, substantial efforts have gone into developing MHD solvers with SPH (Dolag
L118@P3: et al. 1999, 2002), though the divergence-free condition for magnetic fields is still difficult
L119@P3: to handle (Ziegler et al. 2006). For a grid-based Eulerian approach, studies by Ryu et al.
L120@P3: (1998) and Br¨uggen et al. (2005) have included the magnetic fields passively, i.e., they have
L121@P3: omitted the feedback of magnetic fields to the medium (both in the momentum equation
L122@P3: and energy equation). Consequently, we are not aware of any Eulerian-based cosmological
L123@P3: simulations where magnetic fields are included self-consistently.
L124@P3: In this paper, we present a highly accurate cosmological MHD code, named CosmoMHD,
L125@P3: for cosmological simulations that involve magnetic fields. The outline of our paper is as
L126@P3: follows. We first present an overview of the CosmoMHD code and various physics packages
L127@P3: included in CosmoMHD in §2. We then describe the basic solvers for ideal MHD adopted in
L128@P3: our code in §3. Numerical tests are presented in §4. Further discussions are given in §5.
L129@P3: 2. CosmoMHD Code and Physics Packages
L130@P3: 2.1. CosmoMHD Code
L131@P3: The framework of our CosmoMHD code is based on the combination of the TVD-ES
L132@P3: cosmological hydrodynamics (HD) code (Ryu et al. 1993) and an MHD code on an adaptive
L133@P3-4: mesh refinement (AMR-MHD) grid (Li & Li 2003). We have integrated the cosmological– 5 –
L134@P4: solvers for dark matter, atomic physics and star formation feedback processes in the TVDES code with the MHD solvers in AMR-MHD code for gas dynamics (AMR features are
L135@P4: not utilized in CosmoMHD). The hydro TVD-ES code has been extensively used for cosmological applications, including Lyman-alpha forest (Cen et al. 1994), warm-hot intergalactic
L136@P4: medium (Cen & Ostriker 1999a), damped Lyman-alpha systems (Cen et al. 2003), cosmological chemical evolution (Cen & Ostriker 1999b; Cen, Nagamine, & Ostriker 2005) and
L137@P4: galaxy formation (Nagamine et al. 2000,2001a,b,2004,2005a,b,2006). The MHD code has
L138@P4: been extensively used for astrophysical jet simulations (e.g., Li et al. 2006, Nakamura, Li,
L139@P4: & Li 2006).

L234@P5: The CosmoMHD code integrates five sets of equations simultaneously: the ideal MHD
L235@P5: equations for gas dynamics and magnetic field dynamics [Equations (1) to (6)], rate equations for multiple species of different ionizational states (including hydrogen, helium and
L236@P5: oxygen), the Vlasov equation for dynamics of collisionless particles, the Poisson’s equation
L237@P5: for obtaining the gravitational potential field and the equation governing the evolution of the
L238@P5: intergalactic ionizing radiation field, all in cosmological comoving coordinates. The MHD
L239@P5: code consists of several approaches for solving the MHD (or HD) by high-resolution schemes
L240@P5: with finite-volume and finite-difference methods. The code preserves conservative quantities and the divergence-free condition of the magnetic fields. The code is fully parallelized
L241@P5: with OPENMP directives. The MHD solver can also be used as an hydro solver when the
L242@P5: magnetic fields are zero. We will describe the MHD solvers in more details in §3. The
L243@P5: rate equations are treated using sub-cycles within a hydrodynamic timestep due to much
L244@P5: shorter ionization timescales. Dark matter particles are advanced in time using the standard
L245@P5: particle-mesh (PM) scheme. The gravitational potential on a uniform mesh is solved using
L246@P5: the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) method.
L247@P5: The simulation computes for each cell and each timestep the detailed cooling and heating
L248@P5: processes due to all the principal line and continuum processes for a plasma of primordial
L249@P5: composition (Cen 1992). Metals ejected from star formation are followed in detail in a
L250@P5: time-dependent, non-equilibrium fashion. Cooling due to metals is computed using a code
L251@P5: based on the Raymond-Smith code assuming ionization equilibrium (Cen et al. 1995): at
L252@P5: each timestep, given the ionizing background radiation field, we compute a lookup table
L253@P5: for metal cooling in the temperature-density plane for a gas with solar metallicity, then
L254@P5: the metal cooling rate for each gas cell is computed using the appropriate entry in that
L255@P5: plane multiplied by its metallicity (in solar units). In addition, Compton cooling due to the
L256@P5: microwave background radiation field and Compton cooling/heating due to the X-ray and
L257@P5: high energy background are also included.
L258@P5: We follow star formation using a well defined (heuristic but plausible) prescription used
L259@P5: by us in our earlier work (Cen & Ostriker 1992,1993) and similar to that of other investigators
L260@P5: (Katz, Hernquist, & Weinberg 1992; Katz, Weinberg, & Hernquist 1996; Steinmetz 1996;
L261@P5: Gnedin & Ostriker 1997). A stellar particle of mass m∗ = c∗mgas∆t/t∗ is created (the same
L262@P5: amount is removed from the gas mass in the cell), if the gas in a cell at any time meets the
L263@P5: following three conditions simultaneously: (i) flow contracting, (ii) cooling time less than
L264@P5: dynamic time, and (iii) Jeans unstable, where ∆t is the timestep, t∗ = max(tdyn, 107yrs),
L265@P5: tdyn is the dynamical time of the cell, mgas is the baryonic gas mass in the cell and c∗ ∼ 0.07
L266@P5: is star formation efficiency. In essence, we follow the classic work of Eggen, Lynden-Bell &
L267@P5: Sandage (1962) and assume that the dynamical free-fall and galaxy formation timescales are
L268@P5-6: simply related. Each stellar particle has a number of other attributes at birth, including– 7 –
L269@P6: formation time ti, initial gas metallicity and the free-fall time in the birth cell tdyn. The
L270@P6: typical mass of a stellar particle in the simulation is about one million solar masses; in other
L271@P6: words, these stellar particles are like globular clusters.

L729@P12: Maintaining the divergence-free condition ∇ · B = 0 is important in MHD simulations.
L730@P12: Brackbill and Barnes (1980) find that the non-zero divergence, caused by discretization

L736@P12: the magnetic field variables at the cell-face to keep ∇ · B to the accuracy of machine roundoff error. Recently, this approach has been combined with various modern shock-capturing

L738@P12: constrained transport/central-difference (CT/CD) method that uses cell-centered values of

## Abstract

A second-order Godunov-type finite volume method (FVM) to advance the equations of single-fluid solar wind plasma magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) in time has been implemented into a numerical code. This code operates on a three-dimensional (3D) spherical shell with both non-staggered and staggered grids on the overlapping grid system with hexahedral cells of quadrilateral frustum type. By merging geometrical factors in spherical coordinates into the reformulation of fluxes, flux evaluation is made easy to achieve, and thus many numerical schemes with the total variation diminishing (TVD) slope limiters and approximate Roe solvers intended for Cartesian case can follow in the present context of spherical grid described here.

Abstract A second-order Godunov-type ﬁnite volume method (FVM) to advance

the equations of single-ﬂuid solar wind plasma magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) in

time has been implemented into a numerical code. This code operates on a three-

the overlapping grid system with hexahedral cells of quadrilateral frustum type. By

merging geometrical factors in spherical coordinates into the reformulation of ﬂux-

es, ﬂux evaluation is made easy to achieve, and thus many numerical schemes with

the total variation diminishing (TVD) slope limiters and approximate Roe solver-

s intended for Cartesian case can follow in the present context of spherical grid

described here. At the same time, alternative strategies to ensure a solenoidal mag-

netic ﬁeld, such as projection Poisson (PP) solver, hyperbolic divergence cleaning

(HDC) method derived from generalized Lagrange multiplier (GLM) formulation of

MHD system and constrained transport (CT) method, are employed. In this chap-

ter, an FVM is described exemplarily on a six-component composite grid system by

using a minmod limiter for oscillation control. Additionally, an implicit dual time-

stepping technique is demonstrated to model the steady state solar wind ambient.

Being of second order in space and time, this model is written in FORTRAN lan-

guage with Message Passing Interface (MPI) parallelization, and validated in mod-

eling the large-scale structure of solar wind from the Sun to Earth process (hereafter

called Sun-to-Earth Process MHD model, also STEP-MHD model for brief). To

demonstrate the suitability of our code for the simulation of solar wind ambient

from the Sun to Earth, selected results from Carrington rotations (CR) during di ﬀ er-

ent solar activity phases are presented to show its capability of producing structured

solar wind in agreement with observations.

This MHD model is formulated on a six-component composite grid system free of polar singularities. The computational domain ranges from the solar surface to the super-Alfvénic region. As common to all MHD codes, this code must handle the physical positivity-preserving property, time-step enlargement, and magnetic field divergence-free maintenance. To maintain physical positivity, we employ a positivity-preserving Harten–Lax–van Leer Riemann solver and take a self-adjusting and positivity-preserving method for variable reconstruction. To loosen the time-step limitation, we resort to the implicit lower–upper symmetric Gauss–Seidel method and keep the sparse Jacobian matrix diagonally dominant to improve the convergence rate. To deal with the constant theme of a magnetic field that is divergence-free, we adopt a globally solenoidality-preserving approach. After establishing the solar wind model, we use its explicit and implicit versions to numerically investigate the steady-state solar wind in Carrington rotations (CRs) 2172 and 2210. The governing equations for the solar wind flow and magnetic field utilize the entropy-consistent nine-wave magnetic field divergence diminishing ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) equations, which are symmetric and Galilean invariant with some nonconservative terms proportional to the divergence of magnetic field or the gradient of the Lagrange multiplier ψ. By using solenoidality-preserving and non-negativity-preserving reconstruction, the divergence error is further constrained, and the densities and pressures are reliably guaranteed. Moreover, the entropy is used as an auxiliary equation to completely avoid the appearance of negative pressure, which is independent of any numerical flux and can be retrofit into any MHD equations straightforwardly. All the properties referred to above make the newly developed scheme more handy and robust to cope with the high Mach number or low plasma β situations. After the experiments of the entropy consistency and the robustness of the proposed entropy-stable scheme through two simple tests, we carry out the simulation of the large-scale solar wind structures for Carrington Rotation 2183 (CR 2183) in a six-component grid system with the initial potential field obtained from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager magnetogram by retaining spherical harmonics of degree 50. The comparisons of the numerical results with the remote sensing observations and in situ data show that the new model has the capability to produce structured solar wind.
